utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Carlos Fonseca Sanchez, who is from Colombia and a law student at the El Rosario University Bogota. He's been with the team since the 1st of June this year. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellency. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Dobrijevic.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope, Excellency, that you are aware of the reasons for the delay and that is beyond my control. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dobrijevic, yesterday we were discussing the way crimes are dealt with. Tell us, do you know whether a single crime was hushed up from the level of the criminal police?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any idea as to how many cases you had solved and how many perpetrators had you found -- or, rather, in how many cases did you establish who the perpetrators were?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were reports compiled every day, but it's the criminal register that can show the exact cases involved and that is where we recorded everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any information as to how many cases were completed before the judiciary during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police does not really have that kind of information, because it is the court that is in charge of proceedings and sentencing. Only once all of that is over, records are sent and compiled at the Ministry of the Interior as well, in terms of the sentences concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday we saw one of your plans of work with regard to one particular murder case. Was that an exception or are such plans always made?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Always a plan is made. In the case of grave crimes -- if the Presiding Judge allows me to explain, we had a bit of a misunderstanding yesterday, didn't we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we talked about compiling reports, I did not finish that report because I was sent to the front line. That is what prevented me from doing that. When I looked at the dates I realised it then. In the beginning of September I went to the front line, Novi Grad, and after that, the front line near Sanski Most because by then there was fighting already around Sanski Most. That is why a report was not filed in relation to the person I mentioned yesterday. Otherwise, in operational terms, it was done. It's only the fact that I was absent from the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, did anybody else go on with this work?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Most probably. The entire documentation was there and it could have been used for compiling a report and filing the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know exactly what the number is, but there are 30 cases here that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that had been dealt with at your police station. The document was created on the 24th of April, 2001. Maybe Mr. Robinson can tell us what the D number is. The 24th of April, 2001, that's when the document was created. Do you know how the Kaltak case was finished?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Begic, found in the Sana river?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you expound on that? This doesn't really mean a thing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us -- can you remember the cases that you worked on and that were completed?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to remember. It's been quite a while. Skucani Vakuf, the murder of the Cehic couple and then four or five persons were wounded too, in three houses, I believe. That case was completed. Four persons were part of the report. Two persons with the last name of Mrdja, then one person called Kokot, and then the fourth person was Bilbija -- Bilbija, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D1802, could we please take a look at that in e-court? I believe that the participants can look at the English themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at these first seven that are on the first page. Could you read it to yourself and just tell us whether you know anything about those cases yourself. These are cases that had already been dealt with and that were found at the police station in Sanski Most -- no, in the court, court. So this was already before the court. It says Serb judges here. Once you've read it, could you please tell us so that you can have a look at the next page. Are you familiar with any one of the cases on the first page?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Could we have the next page now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of any one of these cases? It's mostly Croats and Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, there are some Serb names too. Are you familiar with any one of these cases?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at the last page? Do you know that after the war, on the basis of the work done by your service, these prosecutions were completed rather than all of this had not been done in vain?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've already dealt with one of these cases that I referred to a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't remember any one of these cases, Krupic, Jusuf, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, the entire documentation stayed on at the public security station in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't need this document any longer. Could you please tell us, you mentioned some villages. Can you tell us which villages were involved in fighting, Muslim villages? If you like we can call up the map.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the map of Sanski Most? 65 ter 04898, please. Could the witness please be assisted? Could he please be given an electronic pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And could you please mark the Muslim villages here where the population stayed on throughout, and could you explain why?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. Vrse, the village of Vrse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was there? Who lives there?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim population only, and all of them stayed on in Sanski Most until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, could you please mark with the red pen all the villages that stayed on throughout and where there was no fighting?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okrec in part. Part of the population in Fajtovci. Just a moment, please. Is this part here? Because basically local communes are marked here. It's not proper villages that are marked here. Sehovci, the entire population stayed on. And part of the population from some of these places went to Sehovci and lived there from 1992 to 1995, Sehovci, Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I ask you who lived in the village of Gorice and whether the population stayed on?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gorice, Gorice likewise, is near -- above Fajtovci, on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The village of Naprelje?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the village of Naprelje, I've already marked that. Cerici and that part should be there, near Fajtovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Fajtovci, Gornji Kamengrad, Donji Kamengrad?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the population in Gornji Kamengrad stayed on, part of the population, a smaller part of the population, Gornji Kamengrad. Sehovci, everybody stayed on. I cannot find it there, Poljak ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The western part, right? I'm going to read out the names that I have on my list.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sehovci, part of Sanski Most, in the territory of the town of Sanski Most, part of the population stayed on. Yes, Kijevo, Tominska Palanka. Tominska Palanka and Tomina, adjacent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you mark that, please, east?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about Modra, Okrec, you've already mentioned it?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okrec, the entire population stayed on. Modra, Modra, I'm not sure about Modra.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Skucani Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, part of the population stayed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Demisevci?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Dzevari, Husimovci?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Husimovci, part of them stayed on after the voluntary surrender of weapons. And collection of weapons. They left because all of them had relatives in Germany, so they basically went to stay with these relatives. Pobrijezje, quite a few people stayed on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Stari Majdan?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the population in Stari Majdan, a small part of the non-Serb population stayed on in Stari Majdan as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Brdari?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brdari is a Serb village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Trnova?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trnova, I think that no one stayed in Trnova.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Caplje and Zelenkovici [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Caplje, part of Caplje stayed on, part of Caplje, a smaller part of the population, non-Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in these mentioned villages -- and if you're looking at the map, could you please mark this with that red pen because we are going to be needing the black pen afterwards. Was there any fighting in these villages where these people had stayed on?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a police force, as the authorities, how did you deal with these dangers? No, I mean the villages that surrender their weapons, and that were part of your responsibility, if we can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for these inhabitants who stayed on and who voluntarily surrendered their weapons, they were treated just like citizens who were ethnic Serbs. On orders of Mirko Vrucinic, the head of the public security station, police groups were established that provided security for them 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the form of what, patrols, what?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the form of a permanent presence in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With the excess of one murder in Sehovci and individual murders, were there any attacks of any groups against these villages that handed over their weapons, some units?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the pen be changed now, different colour? Could you now mark Muslim villages -- actually we have forgotten the Croat ones, but the Croat ones are there too. Were there any Croat villages that remained intact as well?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes Croat villages remained intact too. And there were persons from these villages who agreed to be soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska. They did so voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you mark the villages where there was fighting? Was there fighting in Klijevca, Hrustovo, Vrhpolje, and other villages?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And part of town Mahala and Muhici, armed conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you mark Hrustovo, do you see where it is?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not a readily legible map. These are hamlets, Kerani, Seferovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mark everything. I have a different map, the ERN number is 03565282, I don't know why they don't show that.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The territory of Kljuc municipality and all the way up to the Sana river, that would be that part. And as for Vrhpolje, Hrustovo, and Galaja forest, this is where they carried out that their manoeuvre and crossed over from Vrhpolje to Hrustovo, i.e. Galaja, that belonged to Hrustovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And part of the Sanski Most town, Mahala, Muhici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you see it, can you mark it, please?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this Hrast or Hrust?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, Hrast is by the river, the Sana river, and this should be here. Zdena is above it. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You used the black pen where there were conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, where there were conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And for the remainder of the municipality, do you remember if there were conflicts with the local population, with the local paramilitary units from Sanski Most, I mean?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand you. Could you please repeat your question? Could you please be more clear? I'm really not very clear on your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the rest of the municipality, did the military and the police of the VRS get in conflict with the local paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But later on, in June, July, and partly August, some of the formations that had remained behind, especially from Galaja, part of those units that didn't go to Bihac tried to cross over to Bihac illegally. And units from Prijedor also crossed Sanski Most which resulted in certain incidents and crimes that happened and that were committed by those groups. There was a murder, Mirko Dosenovic was killed in the village of Fajtovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was Mirko? Who killed him?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirko was an elderly local who lived in Fajtovci. He was killed there, close to Bliha waterfall. I was an inspector on site. A woman was wounded, the perpetrator was unknown, and based on the statements of the eyewitnesses, the survivor and the woman who was with her, stated that they had seen a group of five to six armed men, some wore military uniforms, the other wore civilian clothes, they were armed and they strangled Mirko and left him there. They wounded that woman, they inflicted a serious bodily harm on her, but she survived. First she was treated in Sanski Most and then in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And Mirko, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those villages were of Serb ethnicity. Mirko Dosenovic was also Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with the book, "A Crime is a Crime," by Zilhad Kljucanin and Hazim Akmadzic?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I knew Zilhad personally. We went to the same school. He was a bit younger. I believe that he was born in 1961. He graduated from the grammar school in Sanski Most and then he went on to study in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what he says about Hrustovo, Vrhpolje, and the existence of those units, does it tally with what you know about all that?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that book, he describes Mehmed Alagic as a big hero and army leader, and the part that concerns the Serbian population including myself is mostly lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to read one -- a number of names of prominent Muslims, did you know them? Did they stay on in Sanski Most throughout all that time? Selman Velid, a history teacher?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Smail Sarcevic, teacher?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Nusret Krupic, a merchant?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Omer Krupic, president of the MO or, rather, the local board of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mesud Sabic?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the secretary of the health centre, and later on I believe that he was the head of the Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Savanda?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Savanda worked all that time. He went to on-site inspection with us. He inspected the corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Meliha Alisic?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was Dr. Savanda's wife. Her entire family stayed on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and the accused please slow down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Both of you are required to slow down and put a pause. Mr. Dobrijevic, if you could repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Meliha Alisic, this is where we left it off.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know her. She was Dr. Savanda's wife. She lived in Sanski Most all the time. She was a nurse. And Savanda worked with us. He was an employee at the health centre. He went with us to inspect the bodies and to carry out on-site inspections together with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sulejman Tulundzic?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a football referee. I know him very well and he was in Sanski Most all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Hamid Ceric?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he lived in Sanski Most all the time. He was football player.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ismet Cehajic, the head of dentistry?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know him. He lived in Sanski Most all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Senad Burnic from Husimovci?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him really well. We played together in the same football team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Kadir Smajlovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a policeman. He was my colleague. He was my neighbour as well. He lived in Sanski Most all the time with his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Uzeir Smajlovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He remained in Sanski Most all the time. He was a merchant, actually he was a butcher. He owned a butcher shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Fehim Jakupovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Kamengrad?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He stayed on all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Donji Kamengrad?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ismet Ramic? Mico Meskanov, that was his nickname?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ismet Ramic, yes, he was in Sanski Most all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Farko and Faido Alisic?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were brothers, the brothers of Dr. Savanda's wife and they lived in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They were karate fighters?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Faido was a karate fighter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Reuf Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reuf Hodzic, also known as Nanija, he worked all the time in the payment transaction institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And Aziz Zulic, Ahmed Zulic's father who testified here, did he live in Sanski Most all the time?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the hamlet of Pobrijezje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And Emsud Kamber?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Doesn't ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mumin Ceric, Mesa Hazic, Fajko Hazic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please be asked to read the name slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't have to read the names as a matter of fact. How come that they all stayed on? What is the difference between those who stayed on and led a normal life and those who left? Or who were taken to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please explain, what difference are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what the difference was between those who stayed in Sanski Most and those who left?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certain people left Sanski Most, if they wanted to leave, and if they had somewhere to go. Those people who stayed could work, could move around freely, and enjoy the same conditions as the rest of us who lived there. We lived under the same conditions. You also mentioned Manjaca, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. What was the grounds for somebody to be arrested, investigated and eventually, some of them, taken to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they were -- had military fire weapons, they organised rebellions, they prevented the movement of the military, and certain crimes that targeted mostly the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Of those who were arrested and investigated in Sanski Most itself, do you know how many of them were released after the initial triage and how many were eventually sent to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A majority were released. Many more were released than were sent to Manjaca and they continued to live -- lead a normal life in Sanski Most. Or they could leave if they so wished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When Radio Sana announced that civilians from Mahala should gather at the stadium, were they arrested there, at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please put today's date on the map and could you please initial the map?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit it as a separate Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number D4173, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have quite enough of the documents that you signed but I don't have that much time. I suppose that we will have to take an expert or a witness to classify all that. Thank you very much, Mr. Dobrijevic.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pelic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dobrijevic, your first name is Mile and your nickname is Mima; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And your father's name is Mitar; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And on 24th of May, 2006, you testified as a Prosecution witness in the case of Nikola Kovacevic, also known as Danilusko Kajtez, before the State Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And you testified under an oath to tell the truth; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: In your statement at Question No. 7, you stated that on 25th of May, 1992, there was a decision of the political leadership of Sanski Most municipality to seize illegally owned weapons and military equipment from people; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: This decision of the Sanski Most leadership was an implementation of a previous decision of the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina on mobilisation and disarmament of paramilitary formations and individuals who illegally possess weapons and ammunition, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who issued that decision. However, we complied with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And you are aware, were you not, that radio broadcasts calling for surrender of weapons specified Muslims and Croats, who didn't have a chance against the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. And let me explain why, if you will allow me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was involved in investigations and in our offices we did not have radio sets, so I was not a position to listen to any radio broadcasts or anything else. So I really don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Let's see if I can maybe refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Could we please call up P00725? This is a broadcast of the Sanski Most radio and I would like to play a time code starting in 1 minute and 7 seconds to 1 minute and 40 seconds. And for the benefit of the interpreters, that could be found at transcript pages 1 of both B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... Budimlje, and as well as all of the hamlets around these villages, which have not handed over their weapons, to hand them over to the nearest military unit straight away. Any resistance and opening of fire on members of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina who provoke an armed attack on that village, resulting in great material damage and human casualties for you. You do not have a chance in armed combat, so keep a cool head."

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: This broadcast is only calling for the surrender of weapons of non-Serbs, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand everything, but if you say so, that was the case; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And following the deadline on surrender of weapons, the non-Serb settlements of Mahala, Vrhpolje and Hrustovo were attacked; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were armed conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And although no significant amount of weapons were found, thousands of civilians were captured and Muslims' houses were destroyed and burned down; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you. And if you will allow me, I will tell you why.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Vrhpolje, there was a training camp for non-Serbs, i.e. Muslims. The person in charge of the camp was Amir Avdic, the former JNA captain. They were well-armed, well-trained, and a lot of people gathered there from Sanski Most and from Kljuc. And they had a very good unit and a very well-armed unit. There are records of that as well as reports and notes, and everything else. The commander of that unit was Avdic. His deputy was Hukanovic, Hukanovic whose first name was Arif. The commander of the Intervention Platoon was Ifet Hukanovic, and there were a few others. I could give you the name of all those who were well-organised and who put up armed resistance. They had crossed over from Vrhpolje to Galaja, that part belongs to Hrustovo. During combat, a certain number of Serb soldiers were captured and negotiations ensued, and with the mediation of UNPROFOR, 150 of them in three buses were transferred to Bihac together with their weapons. And one part of that unit headed by Arif Hukanovic remained fighting as guerrilla fighters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Could we please call up P03928? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: This is Sanski Most SJB report on the process of disarming paramilitary formations in the Sanski Most SJB area dated 15th of June, 1992. And let's take a look at paragraph 2 of this report, it states: "The action of peaceful disarming and surrendering of weapons was carried out in the period between 10th of May and 25th of May. During that period, the Muslim and Croatian population handed over only hunting weapons and other legally owned weapons, but illegally obtained military weapons were not surrendered and were concealed, buried on instructions from above." This is what happened in Sanski Most municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Mahala and Muhici.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And this peaceful surrender of weapons was followed with the attacks on Muslim neighbourhood of Mahala, villages Vrhpolje, Hrustovo, and which resulted in a high number of captured non-Serb civilians and the large-scale destruction; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There should be quotation marks. Disarmament should be in quotation marks meaning that just the opposite is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're not giving evidence, and --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this is a quotation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: These inverted commas could be seen by the witness. He has the document in front of him. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, I wasn't quoting that paragraph that Mr. Karadzic is mentioning but second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And now can we please take a look at the following paragraph which is the third paragraph? And it states: "On 25th of May, 1992, this 'disarming,'" under quotations, "was followed by a military action attack against the downtown neighbourhood of Mahala which resulted in the capture of 2.000 civilians but no significant amount of weapons have been found because they had been concealed earlier. Several days later, there was a synchronised attack on the Muslim villages of Vrhpolje and Hrustovo. On that occasion, a Muslim force of about 800 men was broken up and militarily defeated while the houses were destroyed and burnt down. So the report of the Sanski Most SJB, the SJB that you worked for, confirms that these attacks on non-Serb settlements resulted in a high number of captured non-Serb civilians and a large-scale destruction, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The terminology that was used in the document is not good but the document is what it is. I have a problem with the terminology. There were no arrests of civilians. There was no need to arrest civilians. Who is the author of this document? I really don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Well, take a look at the last page, please. That's the SJB chief, Mirko Vrucinic. Both in B/C/S and in English. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Somebody signed this on behalf of Mirko Vrucinic. He didn't do it himself. Please take a closer look. You will see the word "Za" and "chief" and then somebody's signature.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we also see the stamp? Could the stamp please be displayed and enlarged?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dobrijevic, this is the stamp of the SJB Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we would need to provide an expert opinion on that because on the basis of this, I really cannot tell whose stamp this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow this. Could we collapse the English? But before we do that, it's a usual thing, somebody else signs something on behalf of the chief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we zoom in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but this here, Mirko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it that you are arguing that this document is fabricated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no, no, I cannot state that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Do you agree that this is an SJB stamp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document should be submitted to a handwriting expertise. I cannot say whether it is that stamp or not. I would not want to go either way in my opinion or just -- or speculate.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please be asked to repeat his remark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear your intervention, but I would ask Ms. Pelic to continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: I would like to move to the detention facilities and interrogations of the detained non-Serbs. At questions 11 and 12 of your statement you state that the type of persons who were taken into custody and that the -- the facilities they were taken in which included Betonirka and the gym at the Hasan Kikic school. In your BiH testimony, you testified to Drago Vujanic, an employee of the Sanski Most SJB, was in charge of prisons of Hasan Kikic and Betonirka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A correction. It's not Hasan Brkic but it's Hasan Kikic, in the Mahala street -- no, no, in the Kljucka Street, Hasan Kikic. Yes, for a brief period of time, it was a kind of collection centre or investigation centre, for a very brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And Drago Vujanic was a chief of those prisons at the time and he was an employee of the Sanski Most SJB; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Drago Vujanic was an employee at the Sanski Most Public Security Station and he was in charge of the people who were detained there, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it that the parties and the staff were waiting from 9.00 so I think it's time to have a break. We will have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Pelic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, just before the break, you confirmed that Drago Vujanic, employee of the SJB Sanski Most, was in charge of the Hasan Kikic and Betonirka prisons. And Mr. Vujanic was appointed warden of these prisons by the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Sanski Most, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably yes. I don't know. He was aware of the document that he signed and what it is. We each get the decision individually, so I really couldn't say "yes" or "no" to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Could we please call up P02639?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, these are conclusions of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Sanski Most dated 4th of June, 1992. And if you take a look at item number 2, it states: The Crisis Staff hereby decides to appoint Drago Vujanic prison warden. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were one of the SJB Sanski Most's employees who interviewed these detained persons, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And in order to interview them, you went to Hasan Kikic school and to Betonirka too; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: People were brought to these prisons in -- by both the army and the police without any basis, without any need; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't quite agree with your assertion. I mentioned this earlier: Those who were brought in were those who had military weaponry or who took part in organising rebellions, attacks on the army and so on and so forth. Mostly those persons were the subjects of an investigation. It could have happened that someone was perhaps not involved in that, but then those persons would be interviewed or interrogated and then released.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: In your BiH testimony at - that's 65 ter 25714, English page 51 and B/C/S page 41 - you testified, and I quote: "Maybe not all rules were obeyed at the time, since some of these people were -- we could not -- I could not even explain myself how they got there, who brought them in and how. Simply, some citizens were brought in by the army, some by the police, without any knowledge on our part and, in my opinion, without any need." That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I provided a similar answer here also.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Now, these persons who were captured were placed in three alleged categories. First one, politicians; second one, nationalist extremists; and third one, persons unwelcome in Sanski Most municipality. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about that. I was in charge of investigations, so our investigations mostly focused on military organisation, procurement of military weapons, attacks on the army, interfering with army movements and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Could we please -- could you please take a look -- the document is still on, it's P02639. Please take a look at item number 1 and it states: Mirko Vrucinic, Nedeljko Rasula, and Colonel Anicic shall be in charge of resolving the issue of prisoners and their categorisation and deportation to Manjaca. First category, politicians. Second category, nationalist extremists. Third category, people unwelcome in Sanski Most municipality." This document reflects what you and your SJB colleagues' task was at the time, not to determine if the detained non-Serbs committed criminal offences but to categorise them and deport them to Manjaca pursuant to the conclusions of the Sanski Most Crisis Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Conclusions are conclusions. However, I said what it was that I did. I cannot speak here on behalf of the people that you refer to here. I was just telling you how I proceeded and what I did. I did not make any decisions about subsequent triage, as I would refer to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Mirko Vrucinic was the chief of the SJB at the time and your boss; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Majkic and then Mirko Vrucinic. On the 4th of June, it was Mirko Vrucinic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, many, if not most, of these detained civilians were from -- there was no evidence that they convicted or participated in the so-called armed rebellion, haven't they?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that. Most of them possessed weapons or took part in the armed rebellions or attacks on the army or preventing army movements and so on and so forth, which, in itself -- the fact that we confiscated over 1.000 pieces of illegally obtained weaponry speaks for itself. Plus explosives, explosive devices, other combat equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Could we please call up P03929?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is the 1st Krajina Corps command state of combat morale in the 1ST KK Unit for August 1992 report and it's dated 3rd of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 3 in English, bottom, and page 4 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: In B/C/S you can see it at the bottom, last paragraph. And I quote: "Certain tensions are still present in Kotor Varos, Kljuc, Sanski Most, and Prijedor areas because of a large number of arrested citizens for whom there is no evidence or criminal reports that they participated in the armed rebellion." Sir, this report reflects that even as late as August 1992, there were still large numbers of innocent civilians detained, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a military document. An error was made because no criminal reports were written for those who possessed military weapons and other items, and for that reason, this is the reason why this document was written in the first place. I would perhaps agree to a certain extent because we did not write up criminal reports for those who possessed weapons and other types of combat equipment or ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Indeed, of these many, many prisoners, only one, one was charged with a criminal offence in the period from the commencement of the conflict until, let's say, late August 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: This is something you testified in your BiH testimony, and that could be found at 65 ter 25714, English page 25, lines 6 to 18, and B/C/S page 18, middle. You were asked how many of these prisoners were charged with criminal offences starting from April 1992 until late August 1992? And you testified: Only one. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. We set off by writing criminal reports but then the conflict broke out, and in that period the courts were not working. For that reason, we only drafted official notes and suggested that these people would be processed criminally, but I don't know why this never happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And of those people, mostly Muslims and a few Croats were shipped to Manjaca and they were not interviewed; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Could you please clarify? A number of people went to Manjaca who were not interviewed. Most of them were interviewed. A number of persons who were transferred to Manjaca were transferred there from Sanski Most because the conditions were better. Later, we went to Manjaca and did interview those people. So I was there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dobrijevic, could you repeat what you said? After you said: "We went to Manjaca and interviewed those people."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A number of persons who were not interviewed in Sanski Most but were transferred to Manjaca were interviewed. We went there as investigators and talked to them. Also, if we needed to clarify some details with people who had already been interviewed about the illegal movement of weaponry and so on, we did that as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And those people were mostly Muslims and Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And you testified in your BiH testimony that - that could be found in 25714, English page 24, lines 8 to 15, and B/C/S page 17, in the middle - that the reason for this was, and I quote: "Well, it was a large number of people so most probably they could not all be interviewed. There was no time. But they were not interviewed most probably because of the workload and the number of people who were transported up there." It is correct, sir, that it was a large number of people who were transported to Manjaca without any interview?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are lists, precise -- with precise numbers of people who were interviewed and those who were not interviewed. How could we have talked with such a large number of people in Sanski Most? So there is a document stating precisely the number of people who were not interviewed. Most of the people, though, were interviewed in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: I would like to turn now to how these detainees were treated in detention facilities. At question 13 of your statement you state that you and your colleagues treated everyone professionally, very humanely and within the limits of your powers. But, in fact, Mr. Dobrijevic, you were involved in inhuman treatment of detainees; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And, sir --

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: I would like to tender previous excerpt of his testimony that was used. It's 65 ter 25714, English page 24, lines 8 to 15, and B/C/S page 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we look at it?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: If we could call it up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is your BiH testimony in the Kajtez case, and if you look in the middle of the B/C/S and English lines 8 to 15, you testified that it was a large number of people who were not interviewed and transported to Manjaca; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps the quote is incorrect, but it wasn't a large number of people who had been transferred to Manjaca who had not been interviewed. There are lists of people who were interviewed. They were listed by name and these lists are at Manjaca and at the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please do not overlap with the interpretation. Yes, could you repeat your intervention?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: As usually, the translation is not adequate. It was not said in original "a large number of people" but part, part, some of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please read from the middle your answer starting, "Well, it was a large number of people ..."

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a large number of people so probably not all the people.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: I tender this excerpt, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit P6554, Your Honours. Excuse me, P6555, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to go back to the treatment of detainees. You testified that we -- that it's completely untrue that there was inhuman treatment of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And I would request that we go to private session, please, for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, could the Chamber move into private session, briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Could we please call up P6556?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a letter of Danilusko Kajtez sent to Vlado Vrkes. And if you take a look at English page 1 and B/C/S page 1 at the bottom, and then going to page 2, item 8, it states: "You know that at Manjaca, I and a few others liquidated 12 people on two occasions which was ordered and witnessed by Inspector Vujanic, Mico Krunic, who was the warden of the Betonirka prison at the time, Mile and other inspectors. The chief at the time was Vrucinic." Mr. Dobrijevic, this Mile and other inspectors --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let him read it first. Did you find the passage? You said it runs to the next page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps you can just help me find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you take a look at the bottom of page 1 in B/C/S, it starts with: "You know ..." Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see, there is a little asterisk here so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to the second page in B/C/S but it's still first page in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Did you find it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: It's fourth line in B/C/S, sir, at the top. It states: "Mile and other inspectors ..."

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mile and other inspectors. Mile who?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a reference to you and your colleagues who were -- went to Manjaca to interview detainees, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. And I don't see why that would refer to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Among others, you interviewed Mr. Adil Draganovic during his detention, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please show me an official note or something? Either I or Mile Dusenovic, it could be Mile Dusenovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Could we please call up 25744, 65 ter? And if we could go to the next page?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: This is an excerpt of Adil Draganovic's testimony in the Brdjanin case on 13th of May, 2002. And in relation to the letter that we just looked at, P06556, and when asked to whom Kajtez is referring as Mile, Mr. Draganovic testified, and I quote: "I do know that person. That's Mile Dobrijevic nicknamed Mima. He was a crime investigations inspector in the public security station in Sanski Most. When the war stopped and after the Dayton Peace Agreement was signed, he has been the chief of the public security station in Ostra Luka, which is called the Serbian Sanski Most. On several occasions, he led groups to Manjaca. I saw him. He interrogated me at Manjaca. He took part in beatings, the beating of people -- the beatings of people." Mr. Draganovic is identifying you here, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. No. No. I am Mile Dobrijevic. My nickname is Mima, but I did not interview Adil Draganovic. And in Manjaca I interviewed a lot of people, several people. As for Adil Draganovic, I did not interview him. I guess there are notes about all of this. I signed each and every one of my official notes, Mile Dobrijevic, signature. If you allow me, I will explain that. Husinovci -- actually we had different sectors. Everybody worked that their own sectors. I had the following sector: Husinovci, Kamengrad, Gornji Kamengrad, Cirkici, Vrse, Okrec.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Could we please call up 65 ter 22128?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: This is a BiH witness statement of Mirzet Karabeg who testified in this case but was not asked here about you. In a statement given to the CSB Banja Luka on 13 September 1995 - and if we could go to page 10 of English at the bottom and B/C/S page 9 at the top - Mr. Karabeg stated, I quote: "The following men were investigators: Number 1, Brane Sobot; number 2, Mima Dobrijevic; number 3, Brane Macura aka Branci; number 4, Dusko Zoric. These four criminals were responsible for the destiny of many murdered Bosniaks and Croats because they immediately decided who was guilty and who was not, who went to the camp and who did not, and they also decided on the beatings, maltreatment and inhuman treatment of detainees." You are the interrogator identified under item 2, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It's correct that I'm in paragraph 2. However, all the rest is not correct. I mean, not only I but there are other interrogators. Of course, I was employed at the public security station. That was my duty and responsibility. As for all the rest here, well, quite a bit was invented, added. These are not facts. These are just arbitrary opinions, chit-chat. I don't even know what to call it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Authorised official, Ibric Zijad from AID [phon] centre for public security. Could you show me the heading once again?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page number 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not aware of this centre of security services in Banja Luka. I'm not aware of its existence. I worked at the Banja Luka centre of public security, but as for this man --

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were deciding who will be released and who will be sent to Manjaca, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. That is really not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, you --

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I state with full responsibility that that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were involved in the beatings, maltreatment and inhuman treatment of detainees; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I state with full responsibility that that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to one more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember whether or not you interviewed Mizret Karabeg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not interview Mizret Karabeg, since Mizret Karabeg is from town and I was not in charge of the town itself. That is one of the facts, too. Thank you for having put this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But do you remember if he was in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Let's go to one more example.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Could we please call up 65 ter 25715? And if we could go to English page 2, towards middle, and B/C/S page 1, towards bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: This is a BiH statement of Jakupovic Hasan given to Sanski Most Lower Court on 24th of April, 1996. And while describing the time he spent in the garages of the Betonirka detention facility, Mr. Jakupovic stated, and I quote: "At the time, their police inspectors have been taking us out for interrogations on a daily basis. The investigators were Dobrijevic Mile, aka Mima, who interrogated me personally; Dusenovic Mile, Sobot Branko, Stanic Radovan, the judge of this court. They would come every night and take us, the prisoners, out and beat us heavily." You were interrogating detainees in Betonirka; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did interrogate detainees in Betonirka but I claim with full responsibility that this is not true. This is invented. Secondly, a moment ago I mentioned the system of work, and the four of us never worked together.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, you interrogated --

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dobrinko Stojinovic was a colleague who worked with me, who was on my team. The others worked individually with other people. There were teams composed of two persons, one from state security and the other one from public security. And also we never worked during the night. So I state with full responsibility that this was invented.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, you interrogated Mr. Jakupovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. That may have happened, but if I interrogated him, there is an official note that I and my colleague, Dobrinko Stojinovic must have signed. These documents should exist. Here or wherever. Because they stayed in -- stayed on in Sanski Most. I mean we made three copies. One was with the state security, we kept the other copy, and the third one would be in Manjaca because everything was sent up there to Manjaca for further processing. Once again, I state with full responsibility that this is false, this is not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were involved in the beatings of prisoners at the Betonirka detention facilities; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: In addition, Mr. Jakupovic stated, and I quote: "When Dobrijevic Mile, aka Mima, interrogated me, he requested 15.000 Deutschmarks from me, promising me that he would immediately release me from the prison and that he would put me on a list for the convoy to move out from here." And in fact, Mr. Jakupovic did pay you 15.000 Deutschmarks and was in return put on a list for a convoy and then to Travnik on 10th of October, 1992, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That cannot be true. These are terrible fabrications. If I can, I'm going to sue him for this, really. Your Honours, this is so inappropriate. These are blatant lies.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Could we please call up 65 ter 25716? And if we could go English page 1, starting at the bottom, and going to second page, and B/C/S page 1 towards the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: This is a BiH statement of Kalakovic Ismet given in Sanski Most and dated 11th of April, 2001. Mr. Kalakovic stated, and I quote: "I was interrogated by Mile Dobrijevic, aka Mima, son of Mitar, and Branko Sobot, aka Brane, son of Mihajlo. Both inspectors of the SJB Sanski Most. There was another interrogator present in the room with them, aka Delija, his last name was probably Delic, 28, 29 years old, blond, 175 centimetres tall. I was not maltreated on that occasion. A policeman who brought me from Betonirka hit me three times with a stick, but I noticed that it was them who told him when to start and stop hitting me." Again, sir, this is one more description of your involvement in mistreatment of prisoners, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another fabrication. I explained a moment ago that we worked in teams, Dobrinko Stojinovic and I. I never worked on the same team with Branko Sobot in relation to these interviews. So this -- this is untrue. And it's not from the area that I dealt with and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Briefly I would like to deal with the last topic. In paragraph 21 of your statement, you stated that it was the policy and practice of the police in Sanski Most during the war to fully investigate crimes irrespective of ethnicity and you never had instructions to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to the private session briefly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because it was under seal. But you could look at it on your e-court. Probably she is going to put that to the witness. We'll see. Shall we continue, Ms. Pelic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, in Sanski Most as elsewhere, persons accused of crimes against non-Serbs were released from mandatory custody so they could go back to the battlefield; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. At that time I was not working at the court. I was not working at the Prosecutor's office. So I consider the question to be a superfluous one as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at one example. You were familiar with the case of Danilusko Kajtez, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Kajtez murdered eight Croats in Skrljevita in Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nedeljko Maricic was the colleague who dealt with that case so he is more familiar with it. And also it caused imbitterment among the population, so in part we were all aware of it. As far as I know, the case was resolved, an indictment was issued, Kajtez was detained, and another person who was of age, I think, and two minors. I may be mistaken because it was not my case, so maybe I'm making a mistake. I think there were four persons who were accused, two of age and two under age.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And in your BiH court testimony in the case of Nikola Kovacevic, aka Danilusko Kajtez, you confirmed the following - and that could be found at 65 ter 25714, English page 49, lines 13 to 32, and B/C/S pages 36 to 37 - and I quote: "If this is the case of Danilusko Kajtez, we have processed it several times. It is a homicide case with aggravating consequences of the criminal law, meaning that several persons were killed on this occasion. For Nikola and other persons, criminal charges were compiled and forwarded to the Sanski Most Municipal Prosecutor's Office. I believe that the case was later forwarded to the Banja Luka Military Prosecutor's Office when Danilusko was arrested." That's correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I stated, and that is my view. Now, who prosecuted who afterwards, I cannot say. That's why I said "I think." I did not claim anything. I said "I think." But I still stand by this and I think that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: And on 2nd of January, 1993, Kajtez was released from detention and returned to his unit, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of these facts, but I did see Kajtez later on in town. That is to say that he had been released, but when, I really don't know. As for that, you could call the prosecutor and the judge who was in charge of the investigation. You could interview him or, rather, hear him as a witness. This documentation does exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Could I please call up P6557?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there going to be a question in respect to this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dobrijevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask or may I clarify in part the Law on Criminal Procedure that is in force in Republika Srpska as far as detention is concerned, et cetera? Detention goes on until the investigation is carried out. In some cases, the perpetrators --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably Ms. Pelic is going to ask you a question about this document. Could you wait? And then if necessary, I will allow you to expand more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you don't have to. Please continue, Ms. Pelic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, Kajtez was released on his own proposal to be returned to his unit, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where he went on. I don't know about that. If we are talking about legal documents, decisions on ending detention and so on, that we can do. However, where Kajtez went, that is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, second paragraph in the explanation, it states: "On 2nd of January, 1993, the investigating judge questioned the defendants who stated that they wanted to return to their unit and suggested that they be released from custody." It's a fact that Kajtez was released on his own request to return to the unit; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know. I did not take part in all of this. Who is the judge? Investigating judge? Captain Srdjan Porca? Would that be it? I cannot see it well. He could -- I mean, give an answer to that, why he did that, and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance? Is it Srdjan Forca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Srdjan Forca. Yes, yes, Captain Srdjan Forca. So I'm not competent to say anything about this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: If we could call up P06542? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, even the president of the Sanski Most SDS Municipal Board, Vlado Vrkes, and the commander of the 4th Battalion of the 6th Krajina Brigade, Captain Ostoja Curkov [phon], begged the High Military Court in Banja Luka to accept some information that would help it pass a fair judgement on Kajtez, haven't they?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're asking me to do. Really. This is a document from which one can see what they were looking for. They know what they were looking for. There are some mitigating circumstances here that should be taken into account during sentencing or something like that. Well, that is the only comment I can give.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, in fact, Kajtez was not tried for these crimes until 2006 when you testified in that case; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kajtez was tried in Banja Luka, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: In 2006; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when but I know that he was tried.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, you testified in his --

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "I know," that means that I assume because I heard or perhaps I read it in newspapers. There was a trial, and judges are independent in their decisions. Any comment would be unnecessary from me as an inspector. It is not up to me to comment the decisions of a judge or court decisions as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Sir, you testified in this case and that was in 2006; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dobrijevic, do you or did you know personally this Kajtez at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I knew him personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you explain to us what the relation was like between you and this Kajtez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew most of the inhabitants of Sanski Most. There was nothing special about our relationship. We were acquaintances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you remember his letter to Vrkes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The letter was shown to me in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, I'll leave it at that. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dobrijevic, could you please finish the answer about the decision P6557, where Srdjan Forca states the reasons for the end of detention? What did you tell us about the law?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the Law on Criminal Procedure of Republika Srpska, detention is not obligatory. It's an optional category, and it can last for as long as is necessary for the completion of the investigation. There are four conditions under which a person can be detained. He should not influence witnesses, re-offending, leaving the territory or escape or something like that, or the crime must not have been a public threat. I believe that he was remanded in custody for the fourth reason. I'm talking about the law that we implement. I believe that all the conditions were met and there were no grounds to keep him in custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or at least this is what we are doing at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you upload that exhibit again, P6557? This is the question for the parties. I wonder whether we have in our evidence the provision referred to in this decision. The last paragraph in English, the military judge, investigating judge, refers to the Article 191 of Law on Criminal Proceedings. So otherwise, I would like any party to produce that document, together with the English, to the Chamber. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I believe that the Prosecution has it. If not, the Defence will make sure to obtain that document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 191 of the Law on Criminal Proceedings from that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It says here that he requested that. Who can request for the custody sentence to be abolished?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can only be the prosecutor. It cannot be at the defendant's request. All the defendants would request that. It is the prosecutor who makes that proposal to the judge. There has to be a statement of reasons according to which there were no more grounds to keep the person in custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me read the last paragraph to you. "The investigating judge has considered the proposal of the defendants and determined that the grounds for detention stipulated in Article 191, paragraph 1, of the Law on Criminal Proceedings, in accordance with which the defendants were detained, is no longer applicable. The military prosecutor was agreeable to that, which is why I decided, as in the ruling." Were the legal conditions met to abolish the detention?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this a question for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this customary? Does the prosecutor have to agree or can the court decide without the prosecutor's agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the judge's call. Sometimes the prosecutor requests for a person to be detained and the judge doesn't have to accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now let's talk about the identity of that person Mile from that letter. Do you hail from the village of Dusenovici?

utterances.speaker: MILE DOBRIJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm from Suhaca. I.e., I am on the border between Kamengrad, Husimovci, and Suhaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Since Mr. Dobrijevic you referred to the practice in the military court, you just minute ago said: "It is the judge's call. Sometimes the prosecutor requests for a person to be detained and the judge doesn't have to accept that." Can the vice versa be also true? For example, even if the prosecutor requests for a person to be released, does the judge have to -- does the judge not have to accept it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not listen to you carefully. I was not attentive enough. Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said sometimes -- I will read your testimony. "Sometimes the Prosecutor requests for a person to be detained and the judge doesn't have to accept that." So my question is if the prosecutor requests for a person to be released, then does the judge have to follow that suggestion or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the legislation which is in effect now, the answer would be yes, because the prosecutor is in charge of the investigation and they believe that the grounds no longer exist for the person to be remanded in custody. If a request does not arrive to prolong the remand, the person who is being investigated is immediately released because no decision has arrived from the judge. It is the judge who has the right to decide upon the prosecutor's proposal. If the prosecutor does not send that proposal to the judge, a decision cannot be issued to the effect of keeping somebody in custody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
